title: man-memory field line n=16: 16 cells in one room, born by Y

regions.name: input
regions.note: the problem's own stream: `0 addr` (READ) / `1 addr value` (WRITE)

regions.name: router
regions.note: preamble `>rMrbW`: B=op, BP=addr, A=op. Then one walk east — `d` bypasses a lane while BP>0 and peels into it at BP==0. At pitch 4 a lane costs 10 ticks, so one operation is 22+10*addr.

regions.name: cell field (ONE room)
regions.note: all 16 cells share this room — no walls per value. Interior row 0 is the return lane, row 1 the spawner corridor, row 2 the south copy's birth row, rows 3-6 the tiles.

regions.name: spawner corridor
regions.note: `@` starts west of site 0 and walks east. Each `Y` replaces him with two copies born north and south of his heading: the south copy falls through the blank below onto its tile's `>` and is that cell forever, the north copy runs the return lane and drops back here to fire the next `Y`. Residents are therefore born in address order, one per split, and the last copy reaches `H`. Copies retain A/B/BP and nothing is ever loaded, so every cell starts at 0 — no initialisation pass.

regions.name: cell addr 0
regions.note: holds address 0 in its man's B. `r` the command word, `X` on it: 0 walks READ (`W s M`, the `M` restoring B), 1 walks WRITE (`r W`). Identical to the walled cell — only the man arrives by birth.

regions.name: collector
regions.note: `R` takes whichever answer is ready and `s` forwards it to the output, so it needs no pipe affinity at all. Order is safe because the router serves one operation at a time.

regions.name: output
regions.note: one word per READ
